text:
A: Hello? Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
B: Yes, fine. I'm Rana.
A: I'm Denise. I'm in St Helens. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous with these, I never know where to look.
B: Look at the camera, not the screen, that's the trick. I'm in Acton, West London.
A: Oh, right. I'll try that. Erm, what is it you do? If that's alright to ask.
B: I'm a PhD student. Epidemiology. Before that I was a pharmacist for about eight years.
A: A pharmacist? Oh, my mum would love you. She's got that many tablets I've had to get one of those boxes with the days on.
B: A dosette box. Does she actually use it?
A: Mostly. She forgets the evening ones, so I ring her about seven and say, have you had your tablets, and she says yes, and then I go round and they're still in the box.
B: That's literally my thesis. Medication adherence in older people. Sorry, honestly, that's exactly it. There are two things, actually, that come up again and again. One, people feel fine, so they think they don't need the tablet. And two, nobody's ever properly explained what each one is for.
A: That's her. She says, what's this little white one for, and I don't know either.
B: You should ask for a medicines review at the GP, or the pharmacy can do one. They're supposed to go through every single item with her. Most people don't know you can ask.
A: I didn't know that. I'll write that down. I do all her appointments anyway, I'm the only one nearby, my brother's in Devon.
B: Mm. My dad's diabetic and he's terrible with his. My mum hides the biscuits, he finds them.
A: Oh dear. They're all the same, aren't they.
B: Completely. What do you do, Denise?
A: I'm a dental technician. I make crowns and bridges and dentures for the dentists. I've been at the same lab over twenty-five years.
B: Oh, that's very precise work, isn't it? Like, microns?
A: It is, yeah. You've got to get the fit right or it rubs, or it won't go on at all. If the impression's no good I ring the dentist and tell them, I won't bodge it. Some places would, to save money, but I'd sooner do it again.
B: Good. I used to be like that with prescriptions. I'd catch the errors and make sure the manager knew. Not very popular for it.
A: No, people don't always like being told, do they. But it's their teeth, or their tablets, isn't it.
B: Exactly. Do you use digital scanning now, or is it still all by hand?
A: Bit of both. We've got a scanner now, the young lad who's started is better on it than me, to be honest. I'm more the hands side. I'd like to teach him that before I retire, so it doesn't get lost.
B: That's sensible. The hand skills are the bit you can't just download, innit. Sorry, isn't it.
A: Ha, no, you're alright. I say all sorts.
B: What do you do outside work?
A: Oh, nothing exciting really. I walk by the canal, I do jigsaws, I bake for church coffee mornings. Scones, Victoria sponge, that sort of thing.
B: I cook. Iraqi food mostly, dolma, that kind of thing. I'm better than my sister, whatever she says.
A: Oh, I've never had that. Is it hard?
